posts.title: The first drip of the season
posts.excerpt: Every winter one tank is not pressed at all. The mash hangs in cloth bags overnight, and by morning about six hundred bottles' worth has fallen, one drop at a time.
posts.content:
The first Shizuku of the season is never planned to the day. Shun tastes the tank every morning for a week, and one morning he simply says: tonight. By evening the brewers have filled forty cotton bags with mash and hung them from a cedar pole over a small glass-lined tank.

Nothing but gravity

No press, no pressure. What falls through the cloth is the most delicate sake of the year: clear, fragrant, with none of the bitterness that squeezing can bring. By morning the bags hang limp and the tank holds about four hundred litres.

You cannot make it fall faster. That is the whole recipe.

Shun Amane

Small, and gone quickly

We bottle it within a day and keep it cold. Subscribers to The Pressing Letter hear about it first and can reserve one bottle each; the rest goes to the cellar. Please enjoy it slowly: a small glass, lightly chilled, with something simple to eat.

posts.title: Why we polish rice to forty percent
posts.excerpt: Sixty percent of every grain becomes rice flour before Shizuku is brewed. Here is what polishing takes away, what it leaves, and why the number is on every label.
posts.content:
A grain of sake rice has a soft, starchy heart and an outer layer full of protein and fat. The heart gives clean sugar for the yeast; the outer layer gives body, but also rough, earthy flavours. Polishing decides the balance.

Reading the number

  • 65%. Our junmai, taruzake and kimoto: full, savoury, good warm and with food.
  • 55%. Ivory, our junmai ginjo: soft, round, easy at any temperature.
  • 40%. Shizuku, our junmai daiginjo: light, fragrant, a long clean finish.

Lower is not simply better. A well-made junmai at sixty-five percent can be more interesting with dinner than any daiginjo. The number tells you the style, not the quality.

Slowly, or not at all

Our mill runs for about fifty hours to bring rice to forty percent. Go faster and the grains warm and crack. The rice flour is not wasted: local bakers use it for crackers and sweets.

posts.title: Hanging the green cedar ball
posts.excerpt: A ball of fresh cedar sprigs over the gate tells the village that the first sake is pressed. It hangs all year, slowly turning from green to brown.
posts.content:
The sugidama is the oldest sign a brewery has. A ball of fresh cedar sprigs, wired tight and clipped round, hung over the gate on the day the first sake of the season is pressed. When it is green, the sake is new. When it has turned brown, it has rested and mellowed.

Ours is made by Haruko and two neighbours from the cedars on the hill behind the storehouse. It takes an afternoon and most of a large basket of branches.

A calendar you can see from the road

People in Yukimi still read it: bright green in December, olive by spring, brown by the autumn release. Come and see it on a brewery tour, or simply walk past the gate.

posts.title: A winter morning in the koji room
posts.excerpt: It is the warmest room in the brewery and the quietest. For two nights, steamed rice and a dusting of spores become koji, the heart of every sake we make.
posts.content:
At four in the morning the koji room is thirty-two degrees, smells of chestnuts and is lit by one lamp. Shun and a young brewer lift the linen cloth from the rice, break up the clumps with their hands and spread it thin again.

Why by hand

Koji mould grows best when the rice is neither too warm nor too dry, and every batch is different. Hands notice what a thermometer does not: a corner that is getting too hot, a patch drying out. It is the most tiring work in the brewery, and the most important.

Sake is made from rice, but it is decided in this room.

Shun Amane

Visitors on our winter tours can look in through the small window in the door. Please do not come in: we keep the room as clean as a kitchen, and we would rather the koji did not meet anyone new.

posts.title: Sake at an autumn table
posts.excerpt: Grilled fish, persimmon, a little miso and two small cups. How to match our sakes with an autumn supper, and why a small pour is part of the pleasure.
posts.content:
Sake is at its best with food. It softens salt, lifts the sweetness of autumn vegetables and makes grilled fish taste of the sea again. You do not need much: one small flask shared between two through a whole meal.

Three easy matches

  • Grilled mackerel. Cedar Cask Taruzake, cool. The wood and the smoke find each other.
  • Persimmon and soft cheese. Kimoto Three Winters at room temperature.
  • Mushroom rice. Ivory, gently warmed to about 40 °C.

Keep a glass of water beside every cup; we do at the tasting counter. And if someone at the table is not drinking, a warm cup of amazake goes with every one of these dishes.

posts.title: New tasting room hours from August
posts.excerpt: From August the counter is open Thursday to Sunday, from eleven to five, with a new flight from the cellar and step-free access from the gate.
posts.content:
Many of you asked, so from the first of August the tasting room opens on Thursdays too. The counter is now open Thursday to Sunday, 11:00 to 17:00, with the last pour at 16:30.

A new flight

Mio has added The Cellar: kimoto sake after one winter and after three, with a pour from the family's own shelf. It is a quiet way to taste how time changes a sake.

Easier to reach

The gate now has a step-free path to the counter. Walk-ins are welcome for up to three; for four or more, please write to us a day ahead. Drivers and younger guests get amazake on us.

posts.title: Sake lees, the quiet second harvest
posts.excerpt: What stays in the press is not waste. Sake lees season soups, marinate fish and pickle vegetables, and every winter we pack them by hand in paper.
posts.content:
When the sake runs off, the press leaves behind soft white sheets: sake lees, or sakekasu. They are full of rice, koji and yeast, smell of fruit and bread, and have been part of winter cooking in the snow country for centuries.

Three ways to start

  • Soup. Stir two spoonfuls into miso soup with salmon and root vegetables.
  • Marinade. Mix with a little miso and rub on fish or chicken overnight, then grill.
  • Pickles. Bury cucumber or daikon in lees for a few days.

Lees still hold a little alcohol, so cook them through before serving, especially to children. They keep for two months in the fridge and a year in the freezer.

products.name: Shizuku Junmai Daiginjo, 720 ml
products.short: Our quietest sake: rice polished to forty percent, pressed only by its own weight, drop by drop, through hanging cloth bags. Pear, white flowers and a long, clean finish.
products.description:
Shizuku means a single drop. This sake is never squeezed: the mash is poured into cotton bags, hung over a tank and left overnight, and only what falls by itself is bottled. It is the smallest batch we make, about six hundred bottles a winter.

Serve it lightly chilled, in a thin glass, a small pour at a time. Kept in the fridge after opening, it stays bright for about a week.

products.name: Ivory Junmai Ginjo, 720 ml
products.short: Our everyday ginjo: soft melon and steamed rice, a round middle and a dry close. Good cool or at room temperature, with almost any supper.
products.description:
Ivory is the sake our family drinks at home. Gohyakumangoku rice from the fields around the brewery, polished to fifty-five percent and fermented slowly in the cold of January.

It is gentle enough to drink cool and has enough body to warm a little on a winter night.

products.name: Cedar Cask Taruzake, 720 ml
products.short: Junmai sake rested for ten days in a cask of Yoshino cedar. Resin, green wood and a dry, clean edge, like walking into the storehouse in spring.
products.description:
Before glass bottles, all sake travelled in cedar casks and tasted a little of the wood. We keep the old way for one batch a year: ten days in a new cedar cask, then straight into the bottle.

Its dry, woody edge is very good with grilled food and pickles.

products.name: First Snow Nigori, 500 ml
products.short: Cloudy, coarse-filtered sake from the first pressing of the winter: soft rice, a hint of yoghurt and a gentle sweetness. Turn the bottle slowly before pouring.
products.description:
Nigori is sake pressed through a coarse cloth, so some of the fine rice stays in. Ours is bottled from the first tank of the season, in the week the first snow usually falls on Yukimi.

Turn the bottle upside down once or twice, gently, before you open it.

products.name: Kimoto Junmai, Three Winters, 720 ml
products.short: Started the slow kimoto way and rested three winters in the cellar. Toasted nuts, dried apricot and soy, golden in the glass. Lovely gently warmed.
products.description:
Kimoto is the old, patient way to start a sake: the yeast starter is worked by hand with wooden poles and left to find its own balance over a month. This one then waited three winters in our cellar and turned the colour of pale amber.

Try it at room temperature first, then gently warmed to about 45 °C.

products.name: Tasting Trio Gift Box, 3 × 180 ml
products.short: Three small bottles in a paulownia box: Shizuku Daiginjo, Ivory Ginjo and Kimoto Three Winters. Our tasting-room flight, to share at home.
products.description:
The same three sakes we pour in the tasting room's Polish flight, in small 180 ml bottles, packed in a box of light paulownia wood with a card of tasting notes.

A good way to find out which one you like best before you buy a full bottle.

details.Contents: Shizuku Daiginjo, Ivory Ginjo, Kimoto Three Winters
details.Serve: Smallest pours first, chilled to warm

products.name: Hairline Sake Set, flask and two cups
products.short: An ivory porcelain flask and two small cups, each with a hand-drawn line of gold at the rim. Made for us by a small kiln two valleys away.
products.description:
The cups are small on purpose: a few sips each, so the sake never sits long enough to warm. The gold line is painted by hand, so it wavers slightly on every piece.

Hand wash only; the gold does not like the dishwasher or the microwave.

details.Contents: One flask (300 ml), two cups (50 ml)
details.Care: Hand wash; not for the microwave

products.name: Cedar Masu Cups, pair
products.short: Two small square cups of cedar, joined without nails. Hold a glass inside for the old overflowing pour, or use them for salt, sweets or a single flower.
products.description: Masu were once the measuring boxes for rice. Ours are made by a joiner in the next town from offcuts of the same cedar as our casks, and smell of the storehouse for months.

details.Care: Rinse and dry upright; no dishwasher

products.name: Sake Lees (Sakekasu), 500 g
products.short: The soft, fragrant cake left in the press after our junmai sake runs off. For marinades, soups and pickles. Contains a little alcohol, so cook it through.
products.description:
Every pressing leaves behind sheets of sake lees, rich in rice, koji and yeast. We pack them by hand in paper. Stir a spoonful into miso soup, rub it on fish before grilling or use it to pickle vegetables.

Keeps for two months in the fridge, a year in the freezer. Contains traces of alcohol: cook it before serving.

products.name: Linen Tasting Cloth
products.short: The cloth we lay on the tasting counter: unbleached linen with a single drop stitched in gold thread. For drying cups, or as a small runner for two.
products.description: Woven from undyed linen and hemmed by hand, with the brewery's drop stitched in one corner. It softens with every wash.
